title: Neonatal Continuous EEG Monitoring
summary: Neonatal seizures represent the most common neurological emergency in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). An increasing incidence is being observed alongside improved survival rates among preterm infants, a trend partly attributable to the heightened neurological vulnerability of this population. Until recent decades, the diagnosis of neonatal seizures relied primarily on clinical suspicion. However, the improved availability of electroencephalography (EEG) has clearly demonstrated that most neonatal seizures are subclinical, meaning a significant proportion go undetected. Growing evidence supports the use of continuous EEG monitoring (cEEG) to improve seizure detection and more accurately quantify seizure burden. Yet, cEEG is a diagnostically demanding procedure requiring substantial time for the analysis and interpretation of recordings, making it both resource- and time-intensive. Although generally considered non-invasive, the procedure can still be perceived as burdensome given the age and vulnerability of the patient population. The aim of this study is therefore to conduct an audit evaluating the detection rate of neonatal seizures via continuous EEG monitoring, with the goal of establishing this method in routine clinical practice.

interventions.name: Detection of epileptic seizures in high-risk patients—during the first week of life or within one week of the onset of a risk factor—via analysis of one hour of continuous EEG monitoring (cEEG). criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Full-term newborns (born at term) with at least one of the following risk factors: differential diagnosis of paroxysmal events, abnormal neurological findings, detection of electrographic seizures in selected high-risk populations, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE), respiratory or hemodynamic instability, metabolic disorders, surgical procedure, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), sepsis-associated inflammatory injury, initial capillary or arterial pH < 7.1, Apgar score < 5 at 5 minutes, initial capillary or arterial lactate > 7 mmol/L (normal value in newborns < 4 mmol/L)

Preterm infants ≥ 29 weeks of gestation with the following risk factors: low birth weight, respiratory distress syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus with hemodynamic instability (24–48 hours postnatal), periventricular leukomalacia, paroxysmal events, intraventricular hemorrhage, surgical procedure, surviving twin following intrauterine death of the co-twin, infection, premature rupture of membranes or chorioamnionitis, confirmed materno-fetal infection, hemodynamic instability, arterial hypotension, hypovolemia or anemia, twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (donor and recipient twin), necrotizing enterocolitis, anemia, abnormal or suspicious transfontanellar ultrasound findings
Exclusion criteria:
• Children who are older than 4 weeks upon admission to the intensive care unit
• Children who were admitted to other hospital departments
